f.t: The Band describes itself as a sovereign nation that carries its culture forward through strong governance.
The Cahuilla Band of Indians are Mountain Cahuilla, who name themselves Qawishpa Cahuillangnah.
Cahuilla traditional territory spans a large area of what are now Riverside and San Diego counties.

n.l: Anza area, Riverside County, Southern California

s.p: Cahuilla Band of Indians, on its own site
s.t: kuh-WEE-eh (written on the Band's site as kəˊwi:e)

f.t: A nine-member Tribal Council, elected by voting members, governs about 5,400 enrolled members of a confederation of over 30 tribes and bands.
Once at risk of disappearing, Chinuk Wawa is growing again and is actively taught and used in Grand Ronde cultural education.
Grand Ronde federal recognition ended in 1954 and was restored on November 22, 1983; five years later the Tribe regained 9,811 acres of reservation land.

n.l: Grand Ronde, Yamhill County, northwestern Oregon; ancestral ties across western Oregon, northern California and southwest Washington

f.t: The Tribe's Athabaskan language dictionary, Nuu-wee-ya' (Our words), holds about 12,000 entries, and a Talking Dictionary lets learners hear words spoken aloud.
After lobbying Congress, the Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians won repeal of federal termination in 1977.
Siletz is the most diverse confederation of tribes and bands living on a single reservation in the United States.

n.l: Siletz, on the central Oregon coast; ancestral territory across western Oregon into southwest Washington and northern California

f.t: The Museum at Warm Springs shares the history and culture of the three tribes and welcomes visitors in Ichishkiin, Numu and Kiksht.
In 1937 the Warm Springs, Wasco and Paiute organized as one confederated government under their own constitution and bylaws.
Under the 1855 treaty, the Warm Springs and Wasco tribes kept their rights to harvest fish, game and other foods in their usual and accustomed places.

n.l: Central Oregon, stretching east from the summit of the Cascade Mountains
n.n: Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs

f.p: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation
f.t: CTUIR teaches the Umatilla, Walla Walla and Weyíiletpuu (Cayuse) languages to all ages, drawing on the knowledge of fluent speakers.

f.p: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation
f.t: The Tribes restored salmon to the Umatilla River after the fish had been gone from it for 70 years.

f.p: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation
f.t: Nixyáawii, the homeland name used by the Tribes' language program, means the place of many springs.

n.l: Umatilla Indian Reservation in northeastern Oregon, home of the Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla peoples
n.n: Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation

f.t: Graton Rancheria, a federation of Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo groups, regained federal recognition through a law signed on December 27, 2000.
Graton Rancheria launched its own Tribal TANF program serving low-income Native American families in Sonoma and Marin counties.
The Tribe bought about 254 acres just outside Rohnert Park for its reservation.

n.l: Sonoma and Marin counties, California, with a reservation near Rohnert Park

f.t: The Hoopa Valley Tribe runs its own Fisheries Department, which counts the harvest and spawning returns of salmon, steelhead, sturgeon and lamprey.
Tribal fisheries crews made major progress restoring the lower reaches of Supply Creek and Mill Creek between 2015 and 2018.

f.p: U.S. Department of the Interior, Indian Affairs
f.t: The Trinity River carved the Hoopa Valley, and the river has long been at the heart of life on the reservation.

n.l: Hoopa Valley along the Trinity River, Humboldt County, northern California

f.t: The Karuk Language Program teaches all ages through community classes, school partnerships and immersion, linking learners with fluent speakers.
The Karuk People's Center in Happy Camp opened in September 2002 and holds a museum, library, basketweaving classroom and the language program office.

n.l: Klamath River country of northern California, with tribal offices in Happy Camp

f.t: The Kashia Band of Pomo Indians has about 860 members, with its tribal government office in Santa Rosa, California.
The Kashia Band owns the 688-acre Kashia Coastal Reserve, which spans both sides of Highway 1 just north of Salt Point State Park.
Kashia homelands reached from the Gualala River in the north to Duncan's Point, south of the Russian River.

n.l: Sonoma County coast of California, from the Gualala River south toward the Russian River

f.t: Northwest Indian College, with its main campus on the Lummi Reservation, is the only accredited tribal college serving Washington, Oregon and Idaho.
The college grew from the Lummi Indian School of Aquaculture, founded in 1973, and became accredited for bachelor's degrees in 2010.
The Lhaq'temish, the Lummi People, describe themselves as fishers, hunters, gatherers and harvesters of the Puget Sound shores and waters.

n.l: Northernmost coast of Washington State and the waters of Puget Sound, with ancestral lands reaching into southern British Columbia

f.t: The Makah Reservation at Neah Bay sits on the northwest tip of the continental United States.
When a southernmost Makah village was uncovered in the 1970s, artifacts from ancestors who lived 300 to 500 years ago were recovered.
The name Makah came from neighboring tribes and means people generous with food.

n.l: Neah Bay and Cape Flattery, at the northwest tip of Washington's Olympic Peninsula

f.t: Established in 1865, the Morongo Indian Reservation now spans more than 35,000 acres.
Morongo tribal members elect a seven-member Tribal Council to lead their independent tribal government.

n.l: Morongo Indian Reservation beneath the San Gorgonio Mountains, Riverside County, California

f.t: The Muckleshoot Indian Tribe is one of South King County's largest employers, supporting about 3,300 direct jobs.
Muckleshoot speak a dialect of Lushootseed, and tribal language programs teach it to youth to keep it alive.
Among Puget Sound tribes, Muckleshoot is the only one holding rights under two treaties.

n.l: South King County, Washington, in the Puget Sound region; ancestors include Duwamish and Upper Puyallup peoples

f.t: The Nez Perce Tribe in north-central Idaho has more than 3,500 enrolled citizens.
Headquartered in Lapwai, Idaho, the Nez Perce Reservation spans about 770,000 acres.
Nimipuutímt, the Nez Perce language, is a core part of Nimiipuu culture.

n.l: North-central Idaho, with homelands across present-day Idaho, Washington, Oregon and Montana

f.t: One of the most urban tribes in the United States, the Puyallup still fish, hunt and travel the waters of the Puyallup River.
Puyallup tribal members fought for fishing rights in the late 20th century, helping bring about the 1974 Boldt Decision.
The Tribe gives its name as puyaləpabš, meaning people at the bend at the bottom of the river.

n.l: Shores of southern Puget Sound and the Puyallup River, Tacoma area, Washington

f.t: The reservation covers 475,000 acres around Pyramid Lake, which runs about 27 miles long and 11 miles wide.
The Tribe's Language Program offers community Paiute classes, lessons inside schools and meetings with fluent speakers.
The Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe had about 3,014 enrolled members as of May 2024, led by a ten-member Tribal Council.

n.l: Pyramid Lake and its reservation, about 35 miles northeast of Reno, Nevada

f.t: The 208,000-acre Quinault Indian Reservation lies on the southwest corner of the Olympic Peninsula, between mountains and the Pacific.
The Nation has a Taholah Village Relocation Master Plan that includes planning for an upper village, and its Planning Department is updating the plan for 2026.
The Quinault Language Department works to revitalize the Quinault language, with in-person classes in Taholah, Queets and Hoquiam.

n.l: Southwestern corner of Washington's Olympic Peninsula, between the Olympic Mountains and the Pacific Ocean

f.p: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians
f.t: Established on December 27, 1901, the Santa Ynez Reservation began with 99 acres and has grown to more than 1,500 acres.

f.p: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians
f.t: The Tribe's Culture Department founded its language program in 2008, and the Tribe has unveiled a Samala-English Dictionary.

f.p: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians
f.t: Tribal members take part in a historic tomol crossing each year, and the Tribe hosts the annual Chumash Inter-Tribal Pow-Wow and Chumash Culture Day.

n.l: Santa Ynez Valley, Santa Barbara County, California
n.n: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians

f.t: The Swinomish Tribe monitors air quality in partnership with the EPA, with two major oil refineries right next to its reservation.
Swinomish monitors record real-time data on particulates, ozone and nitrogen dioxide, plus weather such as wind, temperature, humidity and precipitation.

n.l: Swinomish Reservation near La Conner, Skagit County, Washington

f.t: The Te-Moak Tribe unites four bands, Battle Mountain, Elko, South Fork and Wells, under one tribal council elected every three years.
Western Shoshone people are descendants of an ancient, widespread people whose name, Newe, means The People.
Traditional Western Shoshone territory took in southern Idaho and the central part of Nevada, among other lands.

n.l: Northeastern Nevada, in Battle Mountain, Elko, South Fork and Wells
n.n: Te-Moak Tribe of Western Shoshone Indians

f.t: Today the federally recognized Timbisha Shoshone Tribe works to keep its language, traditions and sovereignty strong.
The Timbisha, part of the larger Western Shoshone people, have lived in Death Valley and its surrounding areas for thousands of years, and their village sits inside Death Valley National Park.

n.l: Death Valley and surrounding areas of California and Nevada

f.t: The Tolowa Dee-ni' Nation was restored in 1983 through a court case, and its restored government extended citizenship to all Taa-laa-wa Dee-ni'.
Tolowa Dee-ni' language work goes back to a language program formed in 1969, and the Nation calls revitalization vital to Tolowa identity.
Established in 1908 with 160 acres, the Nation's land base was once the largest rancheria in California.

n.l: Smith River and the coast of Del Norte County, far northern California

f.t: The conservancy, a Tongva-led nonprofit and not a tribal government, serves Tongva people, the wider Native community and guests, called kuuyam.
In 2022 Huhuunga, a one-acre parcel in Altadena, was returned to Tongva stewardship. It is now home to the Tongva-led Tongva Taraxat Paxaavxa Conservancy.

n.l: Greater Los Angeles region of California, a homeland called Tovaangar

f.t: The Tulalip Tribes count over 5,100 people, about 2,700 of whom live on the 22,000-acre Tulalip Indian Reservation.
The Tulalip Lushootseed Language Department works toward every tribal home, workplace, gathering and classroom being rich in Lushootseed.

n.l: Tulalip Indian Reservation on Puget Sound, Snohomish County, Washington

s.p: Tulalip Tribes, on its own site

f.t: Me-Wuk culture is alive and widely practiced today, and the Tribe's Acorn Festival has welcomed visitors since October 1966.
Tuolumne Rancheria began in 1910 with 289.52 acres; today the Tribe holds more than 1,700 acres of fee and trust land.
In January 2005 the Tribe opened the Tuolumne Me-Wuk Indian Health Center.

n.l: Sierra Nevada foothills, Tuolumne County, California

f.t: Viejas government rests on participatory democracy, with tribal officials elected by the general council to four-year terms.
Viejas extends its community work beyond San Diego to Kumeyaay relatives in Baja California, Mexico.

n.l: Viejas Reservation in the mountains east of San Diego, California; the wider Kumeyaay homeland reaches into Baja California, Mexico

f.p: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian (American Indian magazine)
f.t: Washoe teachers hold language classes for adults and youth four days a week, and immersion classes reach children in the tribe's Head Start.

f.p: USDA Forest Service, Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
f.t: The Washoe Tribe and its ancestors have made Lake Tahoe their home for at least 2,000 years.

f.p: USDA Forest Service, Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit
f.t: The name Tahoe is thought to come from Da ow ga, the Washoe word for lake.

n.l: Lake Tahoe region and nearby valleys of western Nevada and eastern California
n.n: Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California

f.p: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation
f.t: The Yakama Nation shares an Ichishkiin word each day to help learners build fluency in the language, also called Sahaptin.

f.p: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation
f.t: The Yakama Reservation in Washington State spans about 1,130,000 acres.

f.p: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation
f.t: Arcing around Mount Adams on the Yakama Nation flag are fourteen gold stars and fourteen eagle feathers honoring its bands.

n.l: South-central Washington State, around Mount Adams and tributaries of the Columbia River
n.n: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation

f.t: On June 30, 2026, Save the Redwoods League conveyed 125 acres on Prairie Creek, in the heart of Yurok ancestral territory, back to the Yurok Tribe.
The Tribe's July 28, 2026 release scheduled recreational access at 'O Rew for August 1; the announcement alone does not confirm that opening occurred.
When Yurok people speak of themselves, they say Oohl, which means Indian people.

n.l: Lower Klamath River and the Pacific coast of far northern California, United States
